strings.text.041: Your strategy starts with 60 cards. You can include up to 4 copies of a Common, 3 of an Uncommon, 2 of a Rare, and 1 of a Legendary. Your deck can have no more than 5 Legendary cards in total.
strings.text.043: Start with 30 life and 5 cards in hand. Your base Command Points rise from 3 to 6 over your turns. Unspent points stay available during your opponent's turn.
strings.text.045: Choose your stance and use coordinated attacks, traps, and counters. Reading your opponent matters more than simply attacking at every opportunity.
strings.text.047: At zero life, you enter Life Flame and are protected for that turn. After that, a successful direct attack defeats you. Having to draw when your deck doesn't have enough cards still means an immediate loss.
strings.text.049: During your preparation phase, draw up to 5 cards if you have fewer. The first player skips this on their first turn. Once an effect has fully resolved, discard down to 7 if you're over the hand limit.
strings.text.050: Each player can have up to 4 units, 2 face-down traps, and 1 terrain card. Each unit can carry 1 equipment card. Units can attack as soon as they're summoned, except on the first player's first turn.
strings.text.051: When two attack-position units fight, compare their attack values. The weaker unit is destroyed, and its player takes the difference as damage. A tie destroys neither unit. Against a defending unit, compare attack to defense: a higher attack destroys the defender, usually without hurting its player; a lower attack deals the difference to the attacking player.
strings.text.052: Play counters from your hand when a valid response window opens, paying Command Points right away. You can't sacrifice cards to pay during a response. Once both players pass in a row, the chain resolves from the last effect played to the first.
strings.text.053: These rules are still in development. Check the current card text and in-game rulings for individual effects.

strings.text.066: Watch the videos, then read about the ideas and moments behind the music.
strings.text.070: I wrote the lyrics myself, then used Suno to bring the music to life. It took plenty of prompting and tweaking to get closer to the melody, style, and mood I had in mind.
strings.text.071: The lyrics came to me on an ordinary evening after work.
strings.text.072: I was on a packed Bannan Line train, one hand gripping the handrail in the middle of rush hour. I closed my eyes and imagined I was a bard in the world of The Odyssey, singing to passing travelers about ancient legends slowly fading from memory. That's where these lyrics began.
strings.text.073: The sound was strongly influenced by Two Steps From Hell, Italian pianist Ludovico Einaudi, and Oscar-winning film composer Hans Zimmer. I've always loved their work, from sweeping epic music and tender piano melodies to film scores that make you see an entire scene in your head.
strings.text.074: Their music is also what I often have in my headphones when I'm deep in code.
strings.text.075: So I wanted this theme to be more than background music for a game. I wanted it to hold my own vision of a fantasy world, like a bard's song traveling through the ages, telling a long-lost epic.
strings.text.077: The lyrics for this song came together so quickly that even I was surprised.
strings.text.078: One morning on the train to work, inspiration hit me out of nowhere. In less than five minutes, the first outline of the whole song had formed in my head.
strings.text.079: It started with the Ancient King, a character I created while designing cards built around graveyard mechanics.
strings.text.080: He once ruled a kingdom. Yet even years after his death, people kept praying to him and calling his name, trying to wake him from his long sleep.
strings.text.081: The Ancient King couldn't understand it.
strings.text.082: “I've been dead for so long. Why do you keep calling my name? Why are you still asking a dead man to grant your wishes?”
strings.text.083: There in the train carriage, that question suddenly turned into a series of vivid images in my mind.
strings.text.084: People kneeling before the Buddha. Emperors climbing Mount Tai to perform sacred rites. Monks wearing robes that looked almost like uniforms, with ritual burn marks on their heads that reminded me of crowns or seals of status.
strings.text.085: As those images overlapped, I started wondering: when we call something sacred and keep bowing and praying to it, are we seeking faith, or chasing our own idea of what sacred authority should look like?
strings.text.086: I know these associations and images might make some deeply religious people uncomfortable, or even feel offensive.
strings.text.087: But I have no intention of insulting any religion or belief.
strings.text.088: At its heart, this song was shaped by my own reading and understanding of the Diamond Sutra.
strings.text.089: “All conditioned things are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows.”
strings.text.091: “Let the mind arise without clinging to anything.”
strings.text.092: These passages keep bringing me back to a question: if we let go of our attachment to identity, status, appearances, and the sacred, might everything in front of us take on a different meaning?
strings.text.093: Is an emperor still an emperor after death? Does being worshipped by thousands make someone a god?
strings.text.094: And while everyone keeps asking him to grant their wishes, has anyone wondered whether he has an unfulfilled wish of his own?
strings.text.095: With those questions in mind, I finished the lyrics for Ancient King — The Nameless Wish. Then I used Suno, making adjustment after adjustment until the melody and mood began to match what I imagined.
strings.text.096: Some people might find the lyrics a little wordy. They don't aim for elaborate, beautiful, or especially poetic language. They sound more like an ordinary person thinking out loud.
strings.text.098: I wanted to express my own understanding of an idea: “The Buddha is not bound by the name Buddha; ordinary beings can be Buddhas too.”
strings.text.099: In my imagination, even an ancient king worshipped as sacred by generations of people might, beneath all those titles and halos, simply be someone who once lived, felt joy and anger and sorrow, and had wishes that never came true.
strings.text.100: That's why I kept the lyrics plain and direct, almost like an everyday conversation.
strings.text.101: I wasn't trying to portray an almighty god looking down from above. I wanted to write about a soul still full of questions, even after the world had turned him into a god.
strings.text.102: When everyone is asking the Ancient King to grant their wishes, who is willing to listen to his?
strings.text.103: Royal Knights — In the Wrong Age
strings.text.104: Royal Knights was the first card series I designed, and the starting point for the whole game. So knights, war, protection, justice, and sacred imagery naturally found their way into its world and art, just as they do in so many classic fantasy stories.
strings.text.105: But when I started writing a song for the series, I didn't want to focus on a knight's bravery or the glory of winning a war. I wanted to show a warrior's most vulnerable side, the part he least wants anyone to see before he leaves for battle.
strings.text.106: I wrote the lyrics during breaks at work. It's a little embarrassing to admit, but I was close to tears through most of it. As I pictured the scenes and worked out the words, the emotion just crept up on me. I even worried a coworker would notice and think I'd lost it. Who nearly cries while writing code? Ha!
strings.text.107: Once the lyrics were finished, I gave them to Suno along with the musical style I had in mind, then adjusted the result to find the emotion and atmosphere I wanted.
strings.text.108: The song follows a warrior who knows he won't come home alive once he goes to war. As he says goodbye, he comforts his partner with warmth and conviction. He tells them not to worry, promises he'll return safely, and even says they'll see each other again in spring.
strings.text.109: But he knows better than anyone that he isn't coming back… and he still has to go.
strings.text.110: “Some responsibilities don't let you walk away just because you're scared, heartbroken, or not ready to leave.”
strings.text.111: That's why I built the arrangement around two very different emotions weaving in and out of each other. On one side, there's soaring, powerful music as the warrior keeps reassuring his partner and promising to return in spring. On the other, a female harmony sounds almost like crying, quietly singing the truth he already knows but can't bring himself to say.
strings.text.112: There's a personal reason behind that choice of voices. Traditional stereotypes often expect men to be strong, brave protectors, while women are portrayed as more fragile and in need of protection.
strings.text.113: But I've never thought the line was that clear. Andy Lau even sang a song called It's Not a Crime for a Man to Cry.
strings.text.114: Does wearing armor and carrying a sword mean a warrior isn't afraid of dying? Does being responsible for protecting others mean he never wants to cry?
strings.text.115: What can someone do when they're falling apart inside, but their role, responsibilities, and everyone else's expectations demand that they keep acting strong? Like many people, I've felt that deeply as a father heading into middle age.
strings.text.116: So I chose a female harmony to carry the warrior's most vulnerable inner voice. Not because women are weak, but because I wanted that contrast with the traditional warrior image to reveal a real person beneath the armor, duty, and courage.
strings.text.117: Sometimes the people who look strongest, who always stand in front to protect everyone else, want to be protected and understood too. Sometimes all they need is a hug where they can finally let themselves cry.
strings.text.118: “Life just doesn't always give them that space.”
strings.text.119: So the warrior hides his fear inside his armor and his sadness behind a smile, leaving the person he loves with one last comfort: “I'll come back. I promise.”
strings.text.120: He knows it's a lie. But sometimes the truth is so cruel that he'd rather let them hold on to hope than make them feel the pain of losing him at the very moment they say goodbye. That conflict is where Royal Knights — In the Wrong Age began.
strings.text.121: On one side is a lie he feels forced to tell by duty and circumstance. On the other are the feelings he can't quiet: the struggle, the ache of leaving, and his deepest wishes for the person he loves.
strings.text.122: So even as I wrote those promises that sounded so certain and hopeful, all I could see was a warrior trying to smile while knowing he could never keep them.
strings.text.123: That's how I finished the lyrics, holding back tears. I wasn't trying to write a hero who feared nothing. I wanted to write an ordinary person who was terrified, but still chose to go to war.
strings.text.124: Because sometimes courage isn't about being unafraid. It's about being afraid and having nowhere to turn back.
strings.text.126: A whole world starts with one idea.
strings.text.127: I'm just an ordinary player who loves card games.
strings.text.128: From Magic: The Gathering and Yu-Gi-Oh! to Sorcery: Contested Realm, which I've really fallen for in recent years, card games have been with me since elementary school. Now I'm a father of three, and they've been part of almost every chapter of my life.
strings.text.129: That's probably why one thought has never quite left me:
strings.text.130: “What would it look like if I could design a card game of my own someday?”
strings.text.133: Back When We Had Our Own Shadow Duels
strings.text.134: I'll never forget the “Shadow Duels” my classmates and I played in fifth grade.
strings.text.135: We'd stand on tall chairs to duel, and the winner got to pick any card from the loser's deck and tear it up on the spot. Naturally, you had to finish with Seto Kaiba's most insufferably smug expression.
strings.text.136: Looking back, that rule was completely ridiculous. Ha!
strings.text.137: Watching a card you loved get ripped apart really hurt. But I have to admit, I still remember the sheer thrill of those duels.
strings.text.138: Especially when I was losing and one of my treasured cards was about to be sacrificed to our terrible rules. My brain would go into overdrive: what resources did I have left, what combos could I pull off, and how on earth could I turn this around?
strings.text.139: That feeling of digging for an answer and finally pulling off a comeback is probably one reason I still love card games so much.
strings.text.140: Growing Up Made the Dream Feel Further Away
strings.text.141: These days, I'm a frontend developer (I like to call myself a software engineer). Before that, I spent almost ten years in visual design, including a role leading a visual design team.
strings.text.142: Coding and visual design happen to be two of the skills you need to make a card game.
strings.text.143: On paper, it looked like I had what it took to make this dream happen.
strings.text.144: The problem was, I wasn't that twenty-something with endless time to spare anymore.
strings.text.145: I'm a dad to three kids now.
strings.text.146: I leave early and get home late. During the day I'm an engineer; after work, it's time for the kids and family. By the time everything is done, there's usually very little time left that's actually mine.
strings.text.147: Draw hundreds of card illustrations myself, then write an entire card battle engine from scratch?
strings.text.148: Maybe I could have pulled that off when I was single.
strings.text.149: But now, just thinking about the workload made it feel like this dream would have to wait until the kids had grown up and started lives of their own.
strings.text.150: That could be more than a decade away.
strings.text.151: But I Couldn't Let the Idea Go
strings.text.152: Even so, that urge to create never really went away.
strings.text.153: I really wanted to make a card game of my own.
strings.text.154: The art had to be something I truly loved. Not just illustrations to fill space on a card, but pieces I'd want to frame and hang in my living room, or even put on display in an exhibition.
strings.text.155: The battles had to feel like the card game I'd always imagined. Playing a card should feel natural, counters should reward good decisions, and the interactions and chains between cards should keep giving you something to think about.
strings.text.156: For resources and costs, I also wanted to move beyond the systems I already knew and try something that genuinely fit my own ideas.
strings.text.157: I didn't want to just copy a game that already existed.
strings.text.158: I wanted to pour in all the games I'd played, everything I'd learned, and every little “Wouldn't it be fun if this mechanic worked like this?” I'd collected over the years.
strings.text.159: Still, for someone approaching forty, working full-time and raising three kids, it could feel like a pretty unrealistic wish.
strings.text.160: I'd even joke that I already had one foot in the grave. Was I really going to have to wait until retirement to make this game?
strings.text.161: Then AI Tools Made It Feel Possible Again
strings.text.162: AI has been moving incredibly fast these past few years.
strings.text.163: Like a lot of people, I was curious at first, but also a little skeptical.
strings.text.164: It wasn't until my company started bringing AI tools into our work that I began to understand how much they could actually help.
strings.text.165: They don't necessarily replace creativity or judgment, but they can make it a lot easier to turn an idea into something real.
strings.text.166: And that little universe of card-game ideas, quiet in the back of my mind for so long, started coming together again.
strings.text.168: “If I don't have to do absolutely everything alone, and I can use AI as a tool, could this dream finally be within reach?”
strings.text.169: So I started experimenting in every spare moment I could find.
strings.text.170: Walking to the station each morning, I'd think through card rules and problems the combat logic might run into.
strings.text.171: Once I was on the train, I'd connect remotely and ask AI to build a rough feature or put together a minimum viable prototype to try out an idea.
strings.text.172: Sometimes I'd use a few minutes on a bathroom break at work to add test conditions or adjust what I wanted to check.
strings.text.173: At lunch, I'd look over what AI had produced and see whether the logic matched what I had in mind.
strings.text.174: If it didn't, I'd rethink it, revise the requirements, and go through another round.
strings.text.175: Day after day, I kept repeating that process.
strings.text.176: There were no long, uninterrupted development sessions, and no studio where I could spend entire days creating.
strings.text.177: Just commutes, lunch breaks, and all the little gaps in everyday life.
strings.text.178: At night, after the kids were asleep and I was getting ready to turn in myself, I'd still find myself looking through the artwork I'd loved for years.
strings.text.179: Composition, light, color, atmosphere: I kept searching for the visual style that felt right for this game.
strings.text.180: I don't know how far this will go.
strings.text.181: But at least this time, I'm not just imagining that I'll make a card game someday. I've actually started.
strings.text.183: I know some people don't like AI being involved in creative work, and some want nothing to do with AI-generated art or media.
strings.text.184: I understand that. I used to feel that way too.
strings.text.185: But as I spent more time using AI in my work and creative projects, I came to a conclusion of my own:
strings.text.186: “AI can do a lot of jobs for us. But getting something done and doing it well are two different things.”
strings.text.187: Here's something that happened at work.
strings.text.188: I ran into a very simple logic issue in some code. I figured it couldn't be that hard; I just didn't feel like digging around for the right parameter. So I handed it to AI and used the time to think about other, more important projects.
strings.text.189: When I came back to check the result, I couldn't believe what I was seeing.
strings.text.190: It had added over a hundred lines of code to solve this tiny problem!
strings.text.191: The funny thing was, the code wasn't wrong.
strings.text.192: AI had solved the problem. The feature worked.
strings.text.193: But after reading it, I deleted all those extra lines, went back to the original logic, and changed the trigger condition for a single existing parameter. Problem solved.
strings.text.194: It took me a few seconds.
strings.text.196: It wasn't that AI couldn't solve the problem. It had just taken a much more complicated route than it needed to.
strings.text.197: It did what I'd asked, but it hadn't found what I considered the best solution.
strings.text.198: Of course, maybe I hadn't explained the task clearly enough. If I'd told it to check the existing logic first and avoid adding unnecessary code, things might have turned out very differently.
strings.text.200: AI's abilities matter. So do the experience and judgment of the person using it, and their ability to ask the right questions.
strings.text.203: It can already do plenty of things that used to require a person to handle them directly. As the technology improves, that list will only grow.
strings.text.204: But I've also come to realize that being able to build something doesn't mean knowing why it should be built that way. And solving a problem doesn't always mean choosing the solution that fits best.
strings.text.205: That's where experience, creativity, and judgment really matter.
strings.text.206: Which brings me back to this card game.
strings.text.207: I won't pretend AI hasn't played a huge part in making it. Without that help, given my work and family life, making something on this scale by myself really might have taken another decade or more.
strings.text.208: But I've always known what I wanted to make.
strings.text.209: The art style, the pace of battle, the way resources work, and the chances players should still have to turn things around when a match looks almost lost.
strings.text.210: Those ideas come from years of loving card games, and from constantly thinking, trying things, throwing ideas out, and reworking them throughout development.
strings.text.211: AI helps me turn ideas into something real. My job is to keep asking whether what's in front of me is actually the game I want to make.
strings.text.212: I don't think using AI automatically makes a project good. And I don't think it means the person creating it no longer has to put in the work.
strings.text.213: To me, it's a tool. One that has finally given me a way past the limits of my time and abilities, so I can chase a dream I've had for years.
strings.text.214: AI isn't the reason I wanted to make a card game.
strings.text.215: It's the reason I finally have a chance to make the card game I've been carrying in my heart since I was a kid.

strings.privacy.heading: Crown Islands Privacy Policy
strings.privacy.intro: Thanks for playing Crown Islands. Your privacy matters to us. This policy explains how the game handles your information.
strings.privacy.1.title: 1. Personal Information
strings.privacy.1.body: Crown Islands doesn't require an account. It doesn't actively collect your name, email address, phone number, location, or other information that could identify you.
strings.privacy.2.title: 2. Saved Game Data
strings.privacy.2.body: Your game progress, settings, campaign and chapter progress, and decks are stored on your device. The game doesn't automatically upload this data to the developer's servers.
strings.privacy.3.title: 3. Third-Party Services
strings.privacy.3.body: The game doesn't include third-party advertising, user tracking, or analytics services. It doesn't sell or share players' personal information with advertisers.
strings.privacy.4.title: 4. Internet Access
strings.privacy.4.body: Core gameplay doesn't need an internet connection, and the game doesn't automatically send your game data to the developer's servers.
strings.privacy.5.title: 5. Children's Privacy
strings.privacy.5.body: The game doesn't actively ask children for personal information or knowingly collect their personal data.
strings.privacy.6.title: 6. Changes to This Policy
strings.privacy.6.body: If the game's features or the way it handles data change, we'll update this policy and publish the changes on this page.
strings.privacy.7.title: 7. Get in Touch
strings.privacy.7.body: If you have any questions about this privacy policy, you're welcome to contact the developer.
strings.privacy.site.title: About This Website
strings.privacy.site.local: This website saves your language choice in your browser so it can remember your preference. You can remove it by clearing this site’s browser data. The website has no account registration or developer-added analytics.
strings.privacy.site.video: The website embeds YouTube videos using privacy-enhanced mode. Loading or playing those videos connects to YouTube, whose data handling is covered by Google’s privacy policy. This is separate from the game’s offline gameplay.
strings.privacy.site.host: When this website is hosted on GitHub Pages, GitHub may process technical request information, such as your IP address, to provide and protect its hosting service. See GitHub’s privacy statement for details.

037.effect: Flying. While in attack position, enemy Flying units must attack this unit first.
037.flavor: Even above the thunderclouds, the skies have a sovereign.

038.name: Sky Messenger
038.effect: [Flying]. On entry: you may return another allied unit with cost 2 or less that has not acted this turn to your hand.
038.flavor: It brings news and shows the way home.

039.name: Storm Griffin
039.flavor: Lion's claws tear the line; eagle's wings claim the sky.

040.name: Sunwheel Roc
040.effect:
[Flying]
Your other Flying units gain +1 ATK and DEF.
040.flavor: The shadow of its wings brings early night to a valley.

041.name: Reef Crab
041.effect: While your terrain is Sea, this unit has +1 defense.
041.flavor: After the tide recedes, one rock still moves.

042.name: Sprayfish
042.effect: On entry: you may return another allied unit with cost 1 that has not acted this turn to your hand.
042.flavor: One brief leap reveals the sea's other face.

043.name: Spinefin Hunter
043.effect: May ignore the requirement that a return-to-hand target has not acted this turn. Other targeting restrictions still apply. Does not return itself for free. Returning and summoning the same card again preserves any attack already used this turn.
043.flavor: Its dorsal fin cuts through water—and hesitation.

044.name: Giantclaw River Shrimp
044.effect: On entry: you may return another allied unit that has not acted this turn to your hand. If you do, this unit has +1 defense this turn.
044.flavor: These great claws decide who may cross the riverbed.

045.name: Ink Octopus
045.effect: On entry: target face-up enemy unit has -2 attack this turn.
045.flavor: An unseen enemy is the hardest to strike true.

046.name: Shellshield Turtle
046.flavor: A thousand waves have failed to push this shield back.

047.name: Coral Seahorse
047.effect: On entry: you may return a terrain from your graveyard to your hand. If you do, return another allied unit that has not acted this turn to your hand.
047.flavor: Lost sea charts hide among the branches of coral.

048.name: Sawtooth Shark
048.effect: When attacking an attack-position unit, gain +1 attack for that battle.
048.flavor: Courage charging straight toward it is just to its taste.

049.name: Deep-tide Squid
049.effect: While your terrain is Sea, gain [Guard]. Once during your turn: return another allied unit that has not acted this turn to your hand; if you do, this unit has +2 defense this turn.
049.flavor: Arms rising from the deep can block an entire shipping lane.

050.name: Crown Sea Serpent
050.effect: While your terrain is Sea, gain [Pierce]. On entry: you may change one face-up enemy unit in attack position to defense position.
050.flavor: Where its crown of waves rises, the islands bow.

051.name: Walking Sprout
051.effect: On entry: restore 1 life to your player.
051.flavor: Even across a scorched battlefield, the first new leaf will come walking.

052.name: Spineball Cactus
052.effect: When this unit is broken in battle, your opponent loses 1 life.
052.flavor: Come too close and you will learn why it needs no weapon.

053.name: Ankle Vine
053.flavor: Before rushing ahead, check your ankles.

054.name: Insect-eating Bloom
054.effect: When battling an Insect, gain +1 attack and +1 defense for that battle.
054.flavor: Sweet fragrance does not always lead to nectar.

055.name: Herb Sprite
055.effect: On entry: restore 3 life to your player.
055.flavor: The forest's gentlest power flows through its leaf veins.

056.name: Whipbranch Treant
056.flavor: No branch is beyond the reach of its arms.

057.name: Ancient Thornwood
057.effect: Guard. When attacked in defense position, after battle give the attacker -1 ATK until the end of its controller's next turn. No longer causes life loss when destroyed.
057.flavor: Whoever breaks it always takes a few thorns away.

058.name: Giant Sporeflower
058.effect: On entry: all face-up enemy units have -1 attack this turn.
058.flavor: The flower opens silently, and the will to fight drifts to sleep.

059.name: Forest Elder
059.effect: At the start of your turn, if your terrain is Forest, you may give a face-up allied Plant [Guard] until the end of your opponent's next turn.
059.flavor: It remembers every path, and everyone who needs shelter.

060.name: Worldroot Tree
060.effect: [Guard]. At the start of your turn, if this unit is in defense position, restore 2 life to your player.
060.flavor: Its roots bind the earth to life that refuses to fade.

061.name: Rubble Effigy
061.effect:
When you send this card from the field to the graveyard as a cost to summon a Rock unit, that unit gains [Steadfast] until the end of your opponent's next turn.
Requires the summoned Rock to already allow tribute costs. Does not grant tribute summoning to other Rocks. Hand sacrifices, battle destruction, and other graveyard moves do not trigger it. Multiple copies do not stack. A suppressed material grants no protection; a concealed material can grant it when revealed by being sent to the graveyard.
061.flavor: Even gathered rubble has a will of its own.

062.name: Rolling Boulder Beast
062.effect: Must be summoned in attack position.
062.flavor: Once it starts rolling, taking it slowly is not an option.

063.name: Stone Shieldman
063.flavor: It says nothing, yet makes its defense of the crossroads clear.

064.name: Crystal Sentinel
064.effect: On entry: enemy spells cannot target this unit until the end of your opponent's next turn.
064.flavor: Light passes through crystal, but spells find nowhere to land.

065.name: Canyon Stonefist
065.effect: When summoning this unit, you may send one allied unit to the graveyard to reduce the cost by that unit's printed sacrifice value. Pay at least 1 CP.
065.flavor: After years of silence, the canyon finally clenches a fist.

066.name: Obsidian Vanguard
066.effect: [Pierce]. When summoning this unit, you may send one allied unit to the graveyard to reduce the cost by that unit's printed sacrifice value. Pay at least 1 CP.
066.flavor: Obsidian's point is sharper than a shadow.

067.name: Cliffside Colossus
067.effect: [Guard]. When summoning this unit, you may send one allied unit to the graveyard to reduce the cost by that unit's printed sacrifice value. Pay at least 1 CP.
067.flavor: You face not a guard, but an entire cliff.

068.name: Magnet Golem
068.effect: When battling a Machine, gain +1 attack for that battle. When summoning this unit, you may send one allied unit to the graveyard to reduce the cost by its printed sacrifice value. Pay at least 1 CP.
068.flavor: Every piece of iron that comes close changes its master.

069.name: Volcanic Giant
069.effect: [Bulwark]. When summoning this unit, you may send one terrain on either field to its owner’s graveyard to reduce the summon cost by its printed sacrifice points (minimum 1 CP).
069.flavor: Its footsteps are the thunder forests dread most.

070.name: Sleeping Mountain God
070.effect: [Bulwark]. Must be summoned in defense position. Starting on your next turn, it may voluntarily change position under the normal rules; other card effects may change its position earlier. When summoning it, you may send up to two other units on your field to the graveyard to reduce its cost by their total printed sacrifice points (minimum 1 CP).
070.flavor: Wake the mountain before asking it to move.

071.name: Clockwork Mouse
071.effect: Once during each of your turns: you may search your deck for an Equipment costing 2 or less, reveal it to your opponent, add it to your hand, then shuffle.
071.flavor: Missing workshop parts often turn up in its mouth.

072.name: Rivet Sentry
072.flavor: Even a small rivet can fasten a promise.

073.name: Walking Ballista
073.flavor: Four legs keep it steady. One bow handles the distance.

074.name: Repair Puppet
074.effect: On entry: you may return an equipment with cost 1 from your graveyard to your hand.
074.flavor: Broken does not mean useless. It means its turn has come.

075.name: Steelwheel Chariot
075.effect: While your terrain is Wasteland, this unit has +1 attack.
075.flavor: The rougher the wasteland, the louder its steel wheels roar.

076.name: Drill Vanguard
076.flavor: To learn what lies beyond the wall, drill through it.

077.name: Mobile Rampart
077.effect: [Guard]. While equipped, this unit has +1 defense.
077.flavor: For the first time, a city wall learned to march with the troops.

078.name: Anti-air Battery
078.effect: Ranged. While in attack position, enemy Flying units must attack this unit first.
078.flavor: However wide the sky, a crosshair can reach it.

079.name: Siege Engine
079.effect:
[Pierce]
While equipped, gains +2 ATK for the battle when attacking a unit in defense position.
079.flavor: It was built to answer one question: how thick are the gates?

080.name: Royal Iron Colossus
080.effect: Your other Machines and Warriors have +1 defense. Once per turn, when an equipped allied unit is broken in battle, you may return one of its equipment cards with cost 2 or less from the graveyard to your hand.
080.flavor: The royal city cast its final defense in the shape of a giant.

081.name: Rusted Skeleton
081.effect:
When summoned from the graveyard, cannot attack that turn and gains +1 DEF until the end of your opponent's next turn.
This DEF bonus is a graveyard-summon state, not an entry trigger. Summoning without entry effects still grants it.
081.flavor: The armor is broken. The orders are not yet finished.

082.name: Gravelantern Wraith
082.effect: Flying. Draw 1 card when destroyed in battle. Other ways of sending it to the graveyard do not trigger this ability.
082.flavor: Its lantern lights no road. It searches for lost names.

083.name: Graveyard Keeper
083.effect: While your terrain is Ruins, gain [Guard].
083.flavor: The living may pass, but may not freely disturb the sleepers.

084.name: Carrion Ghoul
084.effect: While either graveyard contains at least five unit cards, this unit has +1 attack.
084.flavor: The quieter the battlefield, the more eagerly it walks.

085.name: Shrouded Guard
085.effect: Enemy traps cannot change this unit's position.
085.flavor: Its stance has not changed in a thousand years.

086.name: Vengeful Cavalry
086.effect: While you have 10 life or less, this unit has +2 attack.
086.flavor: The closer the end, the faster unfinished grudges pursue.

087.name: Soul Lanternbearer
087.effect: On entry: you may return a unit with cost 2 or less from your graveyard to your hand.
087.flavor: A swing of the lantern shows old companions the way home.

088.name: Headless Warrior
088.effect: When this unit is broken in battle, your opponent loses 2 life.
088.flavor: He never looks back, yet remembers every debt.

089.name: Tomb Giant
089.effect: While your graveyard contains at least five unit cards, this unit has +1 attack.
089.flavor: Stories buried beneath the earth form its body.

090.name: Ancient King's Spirit
090.effect: On entry: you may summon up to 2 units, each costing 3 or less, from your graveyard into open slots in defense position, without paying costs or triggering entry effects. Each copy of this card may trigger this only once per turn.
090.flavor: The crown has lost its shine. Its summons still receive an answer.

091.name: Stone-egg Whelp
091.effect: Starting on your next turn after this unit enters play, during your main phase you may send it to the grave; if you do, gain 3 command points.
091.flavor: A crack opens in the rock. Something inside blinks.

092.name: Spark Drake
092.effect: On entry: your opponent loses 1 life.
092.flavor: Its first hiccup lit the entire cave.

093.name: Membrane Drake
093.effect: [Flying]. Once during your turn: you may send this unit to the graveyard. If you do, the next Dragon you summon this turn by paying its summon cost costs 2 less, to a minimum of 1.
093.flavor: Its wings are thin; its longing for the sky is not.

094.name: Marsh Drake
094.effect: While your terrain is Sea, this unit has +1 defense.
094.flavor: Before the reeds stir, it has already slipped underwater.

095.name: Redridge Land Dragon
095.effect: While this is your only Dragon on the field, it has +1 attack.
095.flavor: Even without wings, it makes the earth feel a dragon's might.

096.name: Windcavern Wyvern
096.effect: [Flying]. While this is your only Dragon on the field, it has +2 attack.
096.flavor: The cavern's howl is the prelude to its flight.

097.name: Ironjaw Tyrant
097.effect: [Pierce]. While this is your only Dragon on the field, it has +2 attack.
097.flavor: Its steel-like jaws accept no obstruction.

098.name: Cloudcrest White Dragon
098.effect: [Flying] [Sweep]. If this is the only Dragon on your field, it gains +2 ATK.
098.flavor: Above the white clouds spreads an even brighter wing.

099.name: Furnace Red Dragon
099.effect: On entry: you may send one enemy equipment to the graveyard. While this is your only Dragon on the field, it has +2 attack.
099.flavor: Before approaching, ask how much heat your armor can bear.

100.name: Crown Ancient Dragon
100.effect: [Flying] [Pierce] [Sweep]. If this is the only Dragon on your field, it gains +2 ATK.
100.flavor: It needs no coronation. The mountains already know their king.

101.name: War Cry
101.effect: Target face-up allied unit has +2 attack this turn.
101.flavor: Shout out your fear. Leave your strength upon the blade.

102.name: Shield Formation
102.effect: Target face-up allied unit has +3 defense this turn.
102.flavor: When shields meet, a retreat becomes a line.

103.name: Surge Forward
103.effect: Target face-up allied unit has +1 attack and gains [Pierce] this turn.
103.flavor: One more step forward leaves the obstacle behind.

104.name: Ride the Wind
104.effect: Target face-up allied unit gains [Flying] this turn.
104.flavor: Borrow the wind's shoulder to cross the wall before you.

105.name: Precise Aim
105.effect: Target face-up allied unit gains [Ranged] this turn. Its attack is unchanged.
105.flavor: Take a deep breath until the world has only one point of impact.

106.name: Armor Break
106.effect: Target face-up enemy unit has -2 defense this turn.
106.flavor: Strike the right spot and even thick armor cracks.

107.name: Taunt
107.effect: Change one face-up enemy defense-position unit to attack position.
107.flavor: The easiest foe to lure from behind a shield is an angry one.

108.name: Suppress
108.effect: Change one face-up enemy attack-position unit to defense position.
108.flavor: Make the opponent think about standing steady before advancing.

109.name: Reform the Line
109.effect: Choose up to two face-up allied units and change each one's position once.
109.flavor: A change of position can change the whole battle.

110.name: All or Nothing
110.effect: Target face-up allied unit has +3 attack this turn. At the end of the turn, send it to the graveyard if it is still on the field.
110.flavor: Stake every possibility on this one strike.

111.name: Forestfire
111.effect: Choose one: send a Forest terrain on the field to the graveyard; or give one face-up enemy unit -2 defense this turn.
111.flavor: A moment of light consumes the years the trees remember.

112.name: Chain Lightning
112.effect: Target face-up enemy unit has -2 attack and -2 defense this turn. If your terrain is Sea, you may choose a different face-up enemy unit to give -1 attack and -1 defense this turn.
112.flavor: The water connects more than two reflections.

113.name: Dust Cloud
113.effect: Target face-up enemy unit has -1 attack and loses [Ranged] this turn.
113.flavor: Without a view of the distance, even the finest arrow must wait.

114.name: Headwind
114.effect: All enemy Flying units have -1 attack this turn.
114.flavor: Suddenly, the sky decides to stop helping them.

115.name: Fissure
115.effect: Destroy one face-up enemy unit with cost 3 or less that does not have [Flying].
115.flavor: Even the most reliable ground can suddenly part.

116.name: Entangling Vines
116.effect: Change one face-up enemy unit in attack position to defense position. Until the end of its controller’s next turn, that unit cannot manually change position.
116.flavor: Fold your wings. The forest still has something to say.

117.name: Shatter the Foundations
117.effect: Send one enemy terrain to the graveyard.
117.flavor: Even the grandest battlefield rests upon a foundation.

118.name: Redraw the Battlefield
118.effect: Return your terrain to your hand. If you do, the next terrain you play this turn costs 1 less, to a minimum of 1.
118.flavor: Familiar ground still has another use.

119.name: Terrain Reconnaissance
119.effect: Look at the top four cards of your deck. Add one terrain to your hand, then put the rest on the bottom in any order.
119.flavor: Understand the land before deciding where to fight.

120.name: Road Home
120.effect: Return one terrain from your graveyard to your hand.
120.flavor: A road once traveled need not be traveled only once.

121.name: Disarm
121.effect: Send one equipment on the field to the graveyard.
121.flavor: However tightly you grip, there comes a time to let go.

122.name: Clear the Ambush
122.effect: Choose one enemy set trap and send it to the graveyard.
122.flavor: Once danger is seen, half its power is gone.

123.name: Tidal Pushback
123.effect: Return one face-up enemy unit with cost 4 or less to its owner's hand.
123.flavor: The tide need not defeat you. It only needs to carry you away.

124.name: Bind the Behemoth
124.effect: Target face-up enemy unit with cost 5 or more cannot attack during its controller's next turn.
124.flavor: The stronger the prey, the more chains it deserves.

125.name: Dispel
125.effect: Target face-up enemy unit loses its printed abilities until the end of this turn. Equipment and terrain effects still apply.
125.flavor: Strip away the miracle, and only the body remains.

126.name: Decoy Maneuver
126.effect: Target face-up enemy unit loses [Guard] and has -1 defense this turn.
126.flavor: When the gatekeeper moves, a path appears.

127.name: Melt
127.effect: Send one equipment to the graveyard. Its former host has -1 defense this turn.
127.flavor: Metal remembers that it once flowed.

128.name: Battering Ram
128.effect: Destroy one face-up enemy unit in defense position with current defense 6 or higher.
128.flavor: This weight was made for the thickest wall.

129.name: Banish Remains
129.effect: Exile up to two cards from your opponent's graveyard.
129.flavor: Some stories must truly end here.

130.name: Duel Challenge
130.effect: When an enemy unit declares a cooperative attack: remove all assistants from that attack. The lead attacker continues; the assistants remain on the field but still spend their attack opportunities for this turn.
130.flavor: If you challenge me, step forward alone.

131.name: Pack Supplies
131.effect: Draw two cards, then discard one card from your hand.
131.flavor: The road is long. Leave some room in your pack.

132.name: Deep Exploration
132.effect: Draw two cards. You may cast only one card with this name per turn.
132.flavor: Beyond one more doorway, fortune may change.

133.name: Rummage for Relics
133.effect: Return one equipment with cost 2 or less from your graveyard to your hand.
133.flavor: Beneath the rust waits a blade with work left to do.

134.name: Comrade's Return
134.effect: Return one unit with cost 3 or less from your graveyard to your hand.
134.flavor: This time, I will wait for you to return.

135.name: Call of the Behemoth
135.effect: Look at the top five cards of your deck. You may add one unit with cost 5 or more to your hand, then put the rest on the bottom in any order.
135.flavor: Sometimes a horn's echo returns with footsteps.

136.name: Healing Potion
136.flavor: A small sip of warmth carries you a little farther.

137.name: Emergency Aid
137.effect: Restore 5 life to your player, or 7 if your current life is no more than half your starting life.
137.flavor: In the direst moment, the hands must not tremble.

138.name: Tactical Retreat
138.effect: Return one face-up allied unit to your hand.
138.flavor: Return alive, and you can choose when to strike again.

139.name: Reopen the Grave
139.effect: This turn, you may summon one unit with cost 4 or less from your graveyard, paying its cost. It enters in defense position without triggering its entry effect. Once per turn.
139.flavor: The gate opens once more, but the returning feet must find their footing.

140.name: Last Supplies
140.effect: If your hand is empty after casting this card, draw two cards; otherwise, draw one. You may cast only one card with this name per turn.
140.flavor: At the bottom of the crate lies exactly the hope this moment needs.

141.name: Iron Sword
141.flavor: No legendary name—just a reliable edge.

142.name: Tower Shield
142.flavor: Carry a gate before you, and you can hold a road.

143.name: Battle Axe
143.effect: Equipped unit has +2 attack and -1 defense.
143.flavor: A heavier blade demands a more decisive swing.

144.name: Knight's Lance
144.effect: Equipped unit has +1 attack and gains [Pierce].
144.flavor: Where its point reaches, the line is no longer whole.

145.name: Longbow
145.flavor: Trust strength to the string and choice to the distance.

146.name: Glider Wings
146.flavor: Even without growing wings, one can learn to use the wind.

147.name: Heavy Armor
147.effect: Equipped unit has +3 defense, loses [Flying], and cannot gain [Flying].
147.flavor: Every measure of protection has its weight.

148.name: Guard's Badge
148.effect: Equipped unit has +1 defense and gains [Guard].
148.flavor: Wear it, and stand before your companions.

149.name: Shieldbreaker Hammer
149.effect: When the equipped unit attacks a defense-position unit, it gains +2 attack for that battle.
149.flavor: A shield's confidence cannot withstand repeated blows to one point.

150.name: Skyhunter Crossbow
150.effect: Equipped unit gains [Ranged]. When it attacks a Flying unit, it gains +1 attack for that battle.
150.flavor: Look up. Even the sky has paths worth aiming at.

151.name: Spiked Armor
151.effect: Equipped unit has +1 defense. When it is broken in battle, your opponent loses 1 life.
151.flavor: Even shattered armor remembers how to strike back.

152.name: Traveler's Cloak
152.effect: Enemy spells cannot target the equipped unit.
152.flavor: Dust blurs the outline—and the spellcaster's sight.

153.name: Purifying Charm
153.effect: Enemy traps cannot reduce the equipped unit's attack or defense.

154.name: Mountain Warboots
154.effect: Equipped unit has +1 defense. While your terrain is Mountain, it also has +1 attack.
154.flavor: A firm grip on stone gives strength for one more step.

155.name: Diving Scalemail
155.effect: Equipped unit has +1 defense. While your terrain is Sea, it also has +1 attack.
155.flavor: Resist like scales, and flow with the water like scales.

156.name: Forest Cloak
156.effect: Equipped unit has +1 defense. While your terrain is Forest, it also has +1 attack.
156.flavor: Wear the trees' shadows, and become part of the forest.

157.name: Wasteland Goggles
157.effect: Equipped unit has +1 attack. While your terrain is Wasteland, it also has +1 defense.
157.flavor: When sand cannot blind you, the wilds lose an obstacle.

158.name: Ancient King's Signet
158.effect: Equipped unit has +1 defense. While your terrain is Ruins, it also has +1 attack.
158.flavor: The lost royal seal still wakes memories within stone walls.

159.name: Vampiric Dagger
159.effect: After the equipped unit completes an attack and breaks an enemy unit, restore 2 life to your player if the equipped unit is still on the field.
159.flavor: Each victory preserves another breath for its wielder.

160.name: Decisive Greatsword
160.effect: Equipped unit has +3 attack and +1 defense, but cannot attack players directly.
160.flavor: It seeks an opponent worthy of its weight.

161.name: Tripwire
161.effect: When an enemy non-Flying unit declares an attack: cancel that attack.
161.flavor: One missed step turns a charge into a stumble.

162.name: Spiderweb
162.effect: When an enemy Flying unit declares an attack: cancel that attack. That unit loses [Flying] this turn.
162.flavor: An unseen thread can catch an entire wing.

163.name: Shield Block
163.effect: When an allied defense-position unit becomes an attack target: it gains +3 defense for that battle.
163.flavor: Raise the shield an inch and save one more tomorrow.

164.name: Ambush Thrust
164.effect: When an allied attack-position unit becomes an attack target: it gains +2 attack for that battle.
164.flavor: The real spearpoint waits in the second shadow.

165.name: Mist
165.effect: When an enemy declares a direct attack: cancel that attack.
165.flavor: When the target vanishes, the assault loses its direction.

166.name: Broken Bridge
166.effect: When an enemy unit with cost 5 or more declares an attack: cancel that attack and change that unit to defense position.
166.flavor: Huge footsteps do not guarantee a wide enough road.

167.name: Rockfall
167.effect: When an enemy non-Flying unit declares an attack: it has -2 attack this turn.
167.flavor: When the slope gives way, even bravery slows down.

168.name: Reflecting Shield
168.effect: When the equipped unit is destroyed in battle while in defense position: deal damage to your opponent equal to the amount by which the attack value of that battle exceeded this unit’s defense value.
168.flavor: It remembers every ounce of force you invest.

169.name: Empty Fort Stratagem
169.effect: When an allied unit becomes an attack target: return that target to your hand and cancel the attack.
169.flavor: Leave a shadow to meet the enemy while the true figure departs.

170.name: Guard's Substitute
170.effect: When an allied unit becomes an attack target: change the target to a different legal face-up allied unit, ignoring [Guard] restrictions.

171.name: Shallow Pit
171.effect: After an enemy unit with cost 2 or less finishes resolving its entry effect: destroy that unit.
171.flavor: A wrong first step can end even the shortest journey.

172.name: Behemoth Pitfall
172.effect: After a face-up enemy unit with cost 5 or more finishes resolving its entry effect, if it is in attack position: change it to defense position. It cannot attack this turn.
172.flavor: A welcome prepared for a giant is buried especially deep.

173.name: Warning Horn
173.effect: After an enemy unit is summoned and its entry effect resolves: you may change one face-up allied attack-position unit to defense position. It has +1 defense this turn.
173.flavor: When the horn sounds, it is time to raise your shield.

174.name: Sabotage Spike
174.effect: After an enemy equips a unit: send that newly attached equipment to the graveyard.
174.flavor: A new weapon's greatest oversight is the spike at its feet.

175.name: Foundation Demolition
175.effect: When an enemy plays a terrain: send that terrain to the graveyard.
175.flavor: A new advantage sometimes lasts only until a muffled blast.

176.name: False Intelligence
176.effect: When your opponent activates a trap: play this card from your hand and pay its command cost before resolution to negate that trap effect. Each player may activate only one card with this name per turn.
176.flavor: What the enemy believes need not be the truth.

177.name: Tomb Seal
177.effect: After your opponent adds cards from the graveyard to their hand: look at those cards and exile one of them.
177.flavor: The seal is no decoration. It is the final boundary.

178.name: Equipment Insurance
178.effect: After allied equipment is sent to the graveyard by an enemy card effect or because its equipped unit was destroyed in battle: you may return that equipment to your hand. Each player may activate only one card with this name per turn.
178.flavor: Gather enough fragments, and another chance remains.

179.name: Mutual Doom
179.effect: After an allied unit is broken in battle: if the enemy unit that battled it is still on the field, destroy that enemy unit.
179.flavor: One last grudge catches the victor's stride.

180.name: Comrade's Will
180.effect: After an allied unit is broken in battle: another face-up allied unit has +2 attack this turn.
180.flavor: The fallen pass their unfinished strike to a companion.

181.name: Emergency Supply Crate
181.effect: After an allied unit is broken in battle: draw two cards, then discard one. Each player may activate only one card with this name per turn.
181.flavor: Even in the most chaotic corner, someone left spare hope.

182.name: Last Line of Defense
182.effect: When an enemy declares a direct attack while your life is no more than half your starting life: cancel that attack. Each later direct attack against you this turn deals 2 less damage, to a minimum of 0.
182.flavor: A line held by one is still a line.

183.name: Counterattack Signal
183.effect: After an allied unit is broken in battle: change another face-up allied attack-position unit to defense position. It has +2 defense this turn.
